newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Starbucks coffee shops push ahead in Asia.
newsitem.headline: Starbucks coffee shops push ahead in Asia.

text.p: U.S. coffee firm Starbucks' expansion into Asia is ahead of forecasts and there is still space for robust growth in its key home market, Howard Behar, president of Starbucks Coffee International said on Thursday.
"We've now got three stores in Tokyo and their sales are all about 25 percent above our plan," Behar said in an interview ahead of the opening of Starbucks first shop in Singapore.
He said the company expected to have 15 coffee shops in Japan and 10 in Singapore by September next year.
But Behar said Starbuck's move into Asia did not mean that its U.S. market, where the company has experienced sales growth of between 40 percent to 50 percent a year, was saturated.
"We have about 1,050 stores in the states and there's still plenty of opportunity," he said, adding that Starbucks was planning to open a total of 325 shops in the 1997 fiscal year.
"We don't need to go to the markets. We have $200 million in cash. That's plenty of reserves to fund our growth," he said.
Behar said he had heard that Starbucks' peak Christmas sales in the U.S. were "holding up well."
The company's share price jumped last month after chairman Howard Schultz gave analysts an upbeat appraisal of its sales prospects over the Christmas holiday period.

Starbucks will have invested $10 million in developing its Asian operations by the end of the year, which rises to $20 million if the contribution of its joint venture partners in the region are taking into account, Behar said.
He said he expected the companies' Asian coffee shops to be making a "significant contribution" to the company's earnings in less than five years.
From a low base, coffee demand is rising strongly across Southeast Asia in line with the area's soaring economic growth and the adoption of Western lifestyles by consumers, he added.
Behar said accurate assessments of coffee consumption growth rates in Southeast Asia were hard to find, but estimates focused on increases of between 20 percent to 30 percent a year.

He said coffee drinking was not traditionally a big part of Asian culture but this was changing and Starbucks had partly selected Singapore for its first shop in Southeast Asia because it was the most "Westernised" of the area's cities.
But he said the most crucial part of selecting new locations was the existence of a reliable local partner and this would be a key factor in dictating which other countries Starbucks expanded into.
Behar said the company had evaluated the European market, but felt that Asia offered more potential and it would consider Europe again after it was successful in the Far East.

He said Starbucks was a high quality niche player in the coffee shop market and beverage sales of mainly dark roast coffee made up between 60 percent to 70 percent of its sales and take-away beans and accessories roughly 25 percent.
The company purchases around 70 million lbs (32,000 tonnes) of coffee a year from the highest and most expensive grades.

Currently one container of coffee beans is arriving in Asia every other week to supply the company's shops, but Starbuck's will probably have to build a roasting plant, to complement the existing three plants in the U.S., once the number of shops in the region rises to around 100, Behar said.
